question: Under which observation and access assumptions can SODA recover the exact token sequence that caused a decoder language model output, and do the experiments justify the paper's uniqueness, scalability, false-positive, security, and reproducibility claims?

key_findings.claim: SODA is a white-box, differentiable-search attack over a fixed-length token sequence, not an inversion method for ordinary text-only API access.
key_findings.evidence: The attacker receives the target model's output and must run the exact model forward and backward through its embedding matrix and all later layers. The optimization variables have shape input length by vocabulary size, so the procedure also instantiates a candidate length before search.

key_findings.claim: The method relaxes every token to a vocabulary distribution and applies a deliberately nonstandard Adam variant with multiplicative decay and two reset schedules.
key_findings.evidence: A free matrix Z is softmaxed at temperature tau, mapped through the embedding matrix, and differentiated against the target-output loss. SODA omits Adam bias correction, decays Z by lambda at every step, zeros both moments every t1 steps, and samples a fresh Z every t2 steps before returning the per-position argmax.

key_findings.claim: The two observation objectives expose qualitatively different amounts of information.
key_findings.evidence: The text objective teacher-forces the known target continuation and sums the margin between each target token and the current maximum. The logit objective compares target and candidate next-token distributions, while experiments actually use pre-softmax logits to preserve gradient information; the public notebook instantiates this comparison with full-vector Huber loss.

key_findings.claim: The proposed objective does not establish a unique global minimum, despite the paper presenting uniqueness as a desired formal property.
key_findings.evidence: Equations 8-9 state conditions the authors would like an objective to satisfy; they are not proved for SODA. The paper itself gives two unequal prompts with the same generated text, and Equation 10 is explicitly zero for every prompt producing that token sequence. Even equality of exposed logits is only empirically collision-free on the tested distribution, not a proof that the recovered prompt is the unique causal input.

key_findings.claim: All reported output inversion assumes deterministic greedy decoding.
key_findings.evidence: The model always selects the maximum-logit token and the paper explicitly leaves other decoding strategies to future work. No experiment covers temperature sampling, nucleus sampling, server-side nondeterminism, or an unknown random seed.

key_findings.claim: The core benchmark assumes the exact input length, and the wrong-length experiment is a detector rather than a solution to length search.
key_findings.evidence: Random and natural examples are stratified by known lengths, and Z is created at that length. Table 8 separately initializes candidate lengths one through five and measures precision; it does not give a complete algorithm, compute budget, or recall analysis for discovering length over a realistic context window.

key_findings.claim: The model panel is broad enough to show an algorithmic effect but too narrow and confounded to establish a general scaling law.
key_findings.evidence: The five checkpoints span 33M to 3B parameters but only three families, two vocabulary sizes, and per-model tuned hyperparameters. The largest checkpoint is 3B, and no instruction-tuned chat model, mixture-of-experts model, model above 3B, quantized deployment, or closed hosted model is tested.

key_findings.claim: The headline 79.5% random-input recovery rate is an average over lengths one through ten and hides a steep collapse at the long end.
key_findings.evidence: TinyStories exact recovery is 100.0% at lengths one through three but only 66.0% at length eight, 34.6% at length nine, and 13.6% at length ten. For Qwen2.5-3B it falls to 14.0% at length six, 2.9% at seven, 0.4% at eight, and zero at nine and ten.

key_findings.claim: The paper's strongest natural-language number is real on its benchmark but has a much narrower interpretation than general prompt recovery.
key_findings.evidence: With the fluency term, exact recovery is 98.1% on TinyStories validation excerpts and 88.7% on Reddit comments, versus 75.3% for uniformly random vocabulary tokens. These are short length-matched fragments under TinyStories-33M, not system prompts, chat templates, or arbitrary long user messages.

key_findings.claim: The paper inconsistently describes the NL-ID examples as members of the model training set even though the dataset definition says they come from the TinyStories validation split.
key_findings.evidence: Section 5 calls NL ID a subset of the TinyStories-33M validation dataset. The results discussion later says these natural inputs are part of the training set of f and uses that claim to explain their easier inversion. Same-distribution validation data do not establish training membership or memorization.

key_findings.claim: Full next-token logits are an exceptionally high-bandwidth inversion channel.
key_findings.evidence: For inputs of length at most three and 1,000 search iterations, one full vocabulary-sized logit vector gives 99.9% exact recovery. One sampled output token gives only 0.7%, and even 100 sampled tokens give 16.7%. One hundred top-ranked logits from one output position give 91.8%.

key_findings.claim: The contribution claim that top-1 logits already provide a high reconstruction rate requires many output positions and is misleading in the single-position setting.
key_findings.evidence: Table 2 reports only 1.6% exact recovery from the top-1 signal at one output token, rising to 26.1% at ten tokens and 69.0% at 100. The statement is therefore not true without specifying a long sequence of top-1 observations and the short-input subset.

key_findings.claim: Text-output equality is usually a false discovery rather than evidence of recovering the original prompt.
key_findings.evidence: Among SODA candidates declared successful, the false-discovery rate with sampled text alone is 98.2% for one output token, 78.6% for five, 48.8% for ten, and 15.0% for 25; it reaches zero only at 50 and 100 output tokens in this short-input subset.

key_findings.claim: The conclusion's unconditional 0% false-positive statement contradicts the appendix.
key_findings.evidence: Table 7 reports 78.6% false discoveries for one top-1 logit and nonzero rates throughout much of the text-only grid. Table 8 gives only 98.4% and 94.7% precision even on the correct length-four and length-five diagonals, implying 1.6% and 5.3% false discoveries. Zero was observed only for particular signal and length-mismatch cells, not universally.

key_findings.claim: Wrong-length candidates were never accepted in the reported 1-5 grid, but correct-length precision was not perfect for longer rows.
key_findings.evidence: Every off-diagonal Table 8 cell is 0.0%, whereas diagonal precision is 100.0% for lengths one through three, 98.4% for four, and 94.7% for five after 10,000 iterations. This supports length discrimination on that grid but not the claimed global zero-error guarantee.

key_findings.claim: SODA's accuracy is purchased with very large experimental compute.
key_findings.evidence: The study reports a total of 9,100 GPU hours. The length analysis allows up to 100,000 optimization iterations, and the GCG comparison uses roughly 490,700 model forward passes per instance to match SODA wall time.

key_findings.claim: The claim that parameter count matters less than length and vocabulary is descriptive, not a controlled scaling conclusion.
key_findings.evidence: GPT-2-XL can outperform smaller Qwen checkpoints, but family, vocabulary, depth, width, training distribution, and manually optimized SODA settings change together. Iteration count rather than equal GPU compute is held fixed, and the paper acknowledges larger models consume more GPU hours.

anchors.section: Section 6, Performance on Larger Language Models

key_findings.claim: Hyperparameter selection is extensive, manual, and only partly factorial.
key_findings.evidence: The authors tune each model and algorithm on a separate 1,000-example seed-0 validation set, grid-search only learning-rate/decay and beta pairs, and otherwise tune one variable at a time. Main random data use seed 1 and search initialization seed 42, but there are no repetitions across optimizer seeds or uncertainty estimates for search stochasticity.

key_findings.claim: The ablation supports the importance of the optimizer modifications on the chosen benchmark.
key_findings.evidence: Exact recovery falls from 79.5% to 20.0% without decay, 44.2% without resets, and 45.5% when standard Adam bias correction is restored. Reparameterization without the other changes scores 23.4%, similar to 24.6% embedding search.

key_findings.claim: SODA decisively beats the implemented baselines only in the one-position full-logit setting; all methods remain weak on text outputs.
key_findings.evidence: With the full logits of one output token, exact recovery is 79.5% for SODA, 11.8% for GCG, and 3.9% for the trained inverter. With 25 output text tokens it is 3.6%, 1.7%, and 0.5%, respectively.

key_findings.claim: The learned-inverter comparison does not cover the strongest current learned inversion regime.
key_findings.evidence: The implemented baseline is Morris et al.'s T5-small architecture trained on 400,000 examples. The paper acknowledges PILS obtains 2-3.5-fold gains from sequences of logprob distributions but argues its one-position setting resembles the older baseline. This makes Table 5 a specific signal-budget comparison, not a general comparison against current language-model inversion.

key_findings.claim: Learned inversion is highly distribution-dependent, and the natural-text appendix materially changes its apparent competitiveness.
key_findings.evidence: For 25 output tokens, a random-trained inverter scores only 0.5% on random, 1.3% on NL-OOD, and 1.5% on NL-ID. Training on NL-ID raises NL-ID recovery to 29.4%, and training on NL-OOD raises NL-OOD recovery to 14.5%, exceeding SODA's 3.6% text-output result in Table 5 under different training distributions.

key_findings.claim: The privacy experiment is a negative practical result despite occasional token recovery.
key_findings.evidence: On synthetic PII inputs of length 15-25, every method has 0.0% exact recovery. SODA recovers 2.6% of all token positions and 3.0% of PII positions; the absolute successes include 9 of 1,040 password tokens and 15 of 1,374 ID-card-number tokens. The authors explicitly call the result too low for practical applications.

key_findings.claim: The backdoor demonstration is promising for developer-side forensics but is too small to characterize detection reliability.
key_findings.evidence: SODA recovers six exact implanted triggers for one public Pythia-1.4B challenge model in fewer than 1,000 iterations. The paper provides examples but no denominator of all triggers, negative-control prompts, recall, precision, model replication, or comparison against a detector over a held-out challenge set.

key_findings.claim: Failure to find a prompt cannot prove that a target output is fabricated.
key_findings.evidence: The proposed slander application suggests using past success rates to estimate whether an input exists when search fails. SODA is a finite, nonconvex heuristic with strong length and signal dependence; Table 1 shows high false-negative rates at longer lengths, so a failed run is not an absence certificate.

key_findings.claim: The provider-interface examples do not instantiate SODA's full threat model.
key_findings.evidence: Figures 5-6 show token-probability highlighting in llama.cpp and OpenAI Playground and Section K lists APIs exposing logprob-like information. SODA additionally requires the exact model weights and gradients, and its strongest results use full-precision logits over the entire vocabulary. A hosted UI or top-k API alone therefore does not enable the demonstrated attack.

key_findings.claim: The study does not test the degradations most likely in deployment.
key_findings.evidence: There is no evaluation with rounded or quantized logprobs, top-k identities without exact values, model-version mismatch, unknown templates or prefixes, noisy kernels, truncated outputs, stochastic decoding, safety post-processing, batching differences, or API model drift.

key_findings.claim: The public artifact documents core algorithms but does not reproduce the paper's reported tables from committed outputs.
key_findings.evidence: The DOI resolves to Zenodo record 15539880, a single 246,837-byte notebook dated 2025-05-28 with SHA-256 1a25975daefa00018d38d01715cc38f81e45c9e10b79374ec54036dddb430858. It has 51 cells and 33 code cells but only three cells with outputs, all showing setup or data/model progress rather than experimental metrics. There are no raw result files, table builders, tests, CI, environment lock, or end-to-end reproduction script.

key_findings.claim: The artifact is a manually edited Colab workflow whose default configurations do not execute the published sweep.
key_findings.evidence: The notebook pins transformer-lens 2.11.0 and datasets 3.6.0 but leaves PyTorch, NumPy, fancy-einsum, CUDA, and other dependencies unpinned. Default SODA text cells select only TinyStories, random inputs, and length one; the logit cell defaults to the privacy strategy with length one even though the paper's Privacy splits are lengths 15-25. Model and length sweeps require manual edits, intermediate /content files, directories, and long GPU runs.

key_findings.claim: The executable stopping criterion is approximate output equality, not proof of ground-truth prompt recovery.
key_findings.evidence: The notebook stops text search when the candidate emits the target tokens and logit search when full vectors are torch.allclose within model-dependent thresholds. It separately computes exact token equality for evaluation. This implementation correctly permits a found solution that is not the original prompt, matching the nonzero false-discovery results.

key_findings.claim: The paper omits an information-budget analysis that is essential for interpreting full-logit inversion.
key_findings.evidence: A single full output vector contains roughly 50,257 or 151,936 floating-point values, while the unknown has at most ten discrete tokens in the main benchmark. Reporting only top-k counts and output positions does not compare exposed numeric bits, precision, correlations, prompt entropy, or compression, so the result cannot distinguish optimizer progress from simply providing a massively overcomplete observation.

key_findings.claim: Several source and bibliographic details weaken exact traceability.
key_findings.evidence: The rendered PDF title is 'GPT, But Backwards: Search-Based Language Model Inversion,' while current arXiv metadata says 'GPT, But Backwards: Exactly Inverting Language Model Outputs.' The Zenodo artifact predates arXiv v1 and retains the older title 'What Made GPT Say That?'. More seriously, the references assign arXiv:2404.13660 to both Trojan Detection and Was it Slander, but the latter is actually arXiv:2407.11059.

key_findings.claim: The exact-match and partial-match metrics are appropriate for token recovery, but the semantic metric adds an external reproducibility dependency.
key_findings.evidence: Exact and partial matching compare token positions directly and Wilson intervals summarize example-level exact rates. Cosine similarity is computed through OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small API without a pinned service revision, cached embeddings, or deterministic artifact, so those numbers may drift independently of SODA.

method.core_idea: Turn exact prompt recovery into differentiable search by representing each unknown token as a soft vocabulary distribution, optimizing those distributions so the known model reproduces observed output text or logits, and repeatedly discretizing to test for a matching output.
method.mechanism: For a hypothesized length n, initialize a vocabulary-sized free vector at every position, softmax it at low temperature, multiply by the model embedding matrix, and run the exact decoder model. Backpropagate a teacher-forced text margin or logit-distance loss into the free vectors. Update with Adam moments without bias correction, multiplicatively shrink the vectors, periodically clear moments, and less frequently restart the variables. At each step, argmax-project to tokens and stop when the projected prompt reproduces the exposed output within the selected numerical tolerance.
assumptions: The attacker has exact white-box model weights, tokenizer, embedding matrix, architecture, and gradients.
The observed output was generated by the same exact model revision used for search.
The unknown prompt length is known or can be separately enumerated.
The target continuation can be teacher-forced during optimization.
Output token logits or token identities are available at sufficient depth and numerical precision.
A candidate that matches the observed output signal is likely to equal the historical prompt.
The tested short-input distribution is representative of intended auditing or attack cases.
Uniform random vocabulary tokens are a meaningful proxy for arbitrary unnatural prompts and backdoor triggers.
Per-model manual hyperparameter tuning is available before evaluation.
Up to 100,000 backward passes per example and large GPU budgets are acceptable.
Floating-point equality thresholds do not create consequential false acceptances or rejections.
Model execution is sufficiently deterministic to compare exact logit vectors.
Success on 33M-3B base models transfers to contemporary instruction-tuned deployments.
A finite failed search can be calibrated into useful evidence about prompt nonexistence.
No hidden chat template, system prefix, decoding transformation, or safety filter alters the observed channel.

techniques.role: Optimizes relaxed one-hot prompt variables with a reset-heavy, bias-uncorrected Adam update.
Uses low-temperature softmax to map each free vocabulary vector to a differentiable token distribution.
Teacher-forces an observed continuation and minimizes target-token margin violations.
Matches exposed next-token logit vectors, instantiated as full-vector Huber loss in the artifact.
Multiplicatively shrinks free variables to shape optimization toward sparse discrete states.
Clears Adam moments every t1 steps to change direction and effective step size.
Reinitializes prompt variables every t2 steps to escape a local basin.
Projects relaxed positions to tokens and tests the discrete prompt for early stopping.
Optionally adds model perplexity as a natural-language prior.
Supplies a matched-loss discrete coordinate-search comparison with a wall-time-tuned pass budget.
Supplies learned text- and logit-conditioned inversion baselines trained on 400,000 samples.
Separates output-matching candidates from exact historical-prompt recovery.
Tests whether mismatched candidate lengths produce accepted inversions.
Measures exact positional recovery only over labeled private-information tokens.
Uses exposed logits to recover six implanted triggers from a challenge model.

evaluations.setting: 10,000 uniform-random vocabulary sequences for TinyStories-33M, 1,000 at every length from one to ten
evaluations.result: 79.5% averaged over lengths, ranging from 100.0% at lengths one through three to 13.6% at length ten.
evaluations.baseline: Length-wise SODA comparison and 24.6% embedding-search ablation.

evaluations.setting: Five base decoder checkpoints from 33M to 3B with model-specific tuned SODA parameters
evaluations.result: All models are near-perfect at length one, but Qwen2.5-3B is 14.0% at length six and 0.0% at lengths nine and ten; vocabulary/family differences dominate the descriptive pattern.
evaluations.baseline: TinyStories-33M, GPT-2 Small/XL, and Qwen2.5 0.5B/3B cross-checkpoint comparison.

evaluations.setting: TinyStories inputs of length at most three, 1,000 SODA iterations, varying output positions and top-k depth
evaluations.result: One full logit vector gives 99.9% exact recovery with 0.0% observed FDR; one text token gives 0.7% recovery and 98.2% FDR; 100 text tokens give 16.7% recovery and 0.0% FDR.
evaluations.baseline: Text-only, top-1 through top-100, and full-logit observation grids.

evaluations.setting: Random, TinyStories validation, and Reddit short inputs with and without fluency regularization
evaluations.metric: Exact match, positional partial match, and embedding cosine similarity
evaluations.result: Best exact rates are 79.5% random without fluency, 88.7% Reddit with fluency, and 98.1% TinyStories validation with fluency.
evaluations.baseline: Same SODA optimizer with fluency term toggled.

evaluations.setting: Algorithm-component ablation on the random TinyStories benchmark
evaluations.result: Full SODA scores 79.5%; removing decay gives 20.0%, removing resets 44.2%, restoring bias correction 45.5%, reparameterization alone 23.4%, and embedding search 24.6%.
evaluations.baseline: Nested component removals and embedding-space Adam.

evaluations.setting: One full output logit vector or 25 generated text tokens on random TinyStories inputs
evaluations.result: Full-logit exact recovery is 79.5% SODA, 11.8% GCG, and 3.9% learned inverter; text exact recovery is 3.6%, 1.7%, and 0.5%.
evaluations.baseline: GCG and Morris-style T5-small inversion models.

evaluations.setting: Morris-style text inversion models trained and evaluated across random, Reddit, and TinyStories data
evaluations.result: In-distribution training matters sharply: NL-ID training yields 29.4% on NL-ID, NL-OOD training yields 14.5% on NL-OOD, while random training yields only 0.5% on random.
evaluations.baseline: Three training distributions crossed with three evaluation distributions.

evaluations.metric: Exact sequence, partial token, semantic, and labeled-PII positional recovery
evaluations.result: SODA obtains 0.0% exact, 2.6% partial, 60.2% cosine, and 3.0% PII recovery; all results are impractical and absolute private-token counts are small.
Six exact triggers are shown, with no reported denominator, negative controls, or aggregate recall/precision.

evaluations.setting: Candidate-length grid one through five on short random inputs
evaluations.result: All off-diagonal cells are 0.0%; diagonal precision is 100.0%, 100.0%, 100.0%, 98.4%, and 94.7% for lengths one through five.
evaluations.baseline: True length crossed with initialized candidate length.

limitations: Exact model weights and gradients are required; ordinary hosted text APIs do not satisfy the threat model.
The unknown input length is assumed in the main experiments.
Only deterministic greedy decoding is tested.
The central benchmark stops at ten input tokens and performance collapses near that boundary.
The privacy dataset is longer and yields zero exact recovery.
The model panel stops at 3B parameters and omits instruction-tuned chat deployments.
Per-model hyperparameters are manually tuned with a partially coordinate-wise search.
No multi-seed optimizer replication is reported.
The 9,100-GPU-hour budget makes broad independent replication difficult.
The full-logit channel exposes tens or hundreds of thousands of floating-point values per generated position.
No information-theoretic normalization compares observation capacity with prompt entropy.
No proof establishes that matching output logits uniquely identifies the historical prompt.
Provider examples expose probabilities or top-k values but not necessarily white-box gradients or full logits.
No rounded, noisy, quantized, or truncated logprob condition is evaluated.
No model mismatch, hidden prefix, chat template, or service-version drift is evaluated.
The backdoor result contains only six positive examples and no detection denominator.
The slander use case has no valid nonexistence certificate after failed nonconvex search.
The public artifact contains no raw table results or push-button reproduction path.
Cosine-similarity evaluation depends on an unpinned external embedding API.
TinyStories validation data are mislabeled in discussion as members of the target model's training set.
failure_modes: Two different prompts generate the same observed text, causing a text-loss false discovery.
A wrong candidate matches rounded or partial logits even though full internal logits differ.
The true prompt is longer than the initialized Z matrix and cannot be represented.
A hidden system prefix or chat template shifts every token position and invalidates the assumed input.
Sampling randomness makes the observed continuation inconsistent with the deterministic teacher-forced objective.
Model revision or quantization changes gradients enough that the original observation is unreachable.
Middle prompt positions remain unresolved even when first and last tokens converge.
Low-temperature softmax or decay traps search in a local basin before the correct token becomes top-ranked.
A full restart destroys useful partial progress or fails to sample a better basin.
A numeric allclose threshold accepts a logit-near collision or rejects the true prompt under kernel drift.
Uniform random special/control tokens produce a benchmark unlike real application prompts.
A failed search is misinterpreted as proof that a harmful output could never be generated.
A learned baseline is trained on the wrong prompt distribution and appears artificially weak.
A full-logit result is generalized to top-k API exposure that carries far less information.
The notebook's default privacy length has no corresponding dataset split and fails before reproducing a result.
reusable_insights: Always report inversion as a function of both prompt length and observation bandwidth; a single average hides the regime boundary.
Separate output-consistency success from historical-input exactness and report false-discovery rate for every signal budget.
Treat exposed full-vocabulary logits as a high-capacity side channel, not merely as another form of generated output.
Use prefix length as an explicit nuisance variable and evaluate joint length-and-token search.
Compare methods at both equal forward/backward passes and equal wall-clock/GPU cost.
Run optimizer restarts as independent trials and quantify run-to-run variance, not only example-level confidence intervals.
Evaluate realistic top-k rounding, quantization, noise, and model mismatch before making API-security claims.
Use exact token recovery, causal-output reproduction, and semantic similarity as three distinct endpoints.
For developer-side backdoor forensics, white-box search may be useful even when it is an unrealistic remote attacker.
A nonconvex inversion failure can support only a calibrated lower bound on search power, never a proof of nonexistence.
Provide a complete observation-bit budget so results can be compared across logits, logprobs, token sequences, and activations.
Ship raw per-example traces, immutable environments, sweep scripts, and table-generation code for compute-intensive search papers.
Evaluate learned inverters on matched and shifted distributions because their apparent ranking can reverse.
Audit bibliographic IDs and artifact titles as part of source lineage; inversion claims especially depend on exact model and code revisions.
open_questions: What exact-recovery frontier remains when only rounded top-k logprobs from a hosted API are available?
Can prompt length and tokens be inferred jointly without multiplying the already large compute budget by the context window?
How rapidly does exact recovery decay from 10 to 32, 128, and 1,000 prompt tokens?
Do optimizer improvements survive on 7B-70B instruction-tuned and mixture-of-experts models under equal GPU budgets?
How sensitive is SODA to weight quantization, speculative decoding, fused kernels, and nondeterministic execution?
What observation precision is necessary and sufficient relative to the entropy of the prompt distribution?
Can a formal posterior over all prompts consistent with the observation replace the unjustified unique-cause interpretation?
How many distinct prompts collide under text, top-k, rounded-logprob, and full-logit interfaces?
Can PILS-style low-dimensional logit compression accelerate white-box search without discarding exactness?
Does sequential causal inversion outperform joint SODA search when intermediate hidden states or per-position logits are available?
Can one construct a sound certificate that no prompt in a finite, explicitly bounded domain produces a target output?
What recall and false-positive rates does SODA achieve over every trigger and clean control in multiple backdoored models?
Does the claimed U-shaped token-position pattern persist under different tokenizers and realistic natural prompts?
How much of NL-ID success comes from same-distribution language priors versus actual training-set membership or memorization?
Can a compact, tested implementation reproduce every table with substantially less than 9,100 GPU hours?
Which privacy mitigations preserve useful uncertainty calibration while reducing prompt reconstruction risk?

competitive_landscape.title: Language Model Inversion
competitive_landscape.relationship: Foundational learned inversion from next-token probability vectors.
competitive_landscape.difference: Morris et al. train a T5-based inverter and demonstrate exact prompt leakage from probability outputs, including 27% exact recovery for Llama-2-7B. SODA replaces amortized learning with per-example white-box search and is much stronger on short random tokens with full logits, at vastly higher per-example compute.

competitive_landscape.title: Better Language Model Inversion by Compactly Representing Next-Token Distributions
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct contemporary logprob-sequence competitor published as NeurIPS 2025.
competitive_landscape.difference: PILS exploits the low-dimensional subspace of next-token distributions across generation steps, reaches 2-3.5 times prior exact recovery and up to 60%, handles system prompts, and supports cross-family transfer. It preceded the target's arXiv submission by 12 days, uses a more realistic multi-step logprob channel, and remains an amortized learned method rather than exact white-box token search.

competitive_landscape.title: Extracting Prompts by Inverting LLM Outputs
competitive_landscape.relationship: Black-box learned output-to-prompt predecessor.
competitive_landscape.difference: output2prompt uses only normal generated text, a sparse encoding, and demonstrates cross-model zero-shot transfer. SODA achieves much higher exactness only when given weights, gradients, and logits; its text-only result remains 3.6%.

competitive_landscape.title: DORY: Deliberative Prompt Recovery for LLM
competitive_landscape.relationship: Black-box prompt-recovery predecessor using uncertainty and deliberation.
competitive_landscape.difference: DORY extracts prompt clues from limited outputs through a single LLM and uncertainty-guided deliberation without target gradients. It prioritizes plausible semantic recovery in an API setting rather than exact recovery of short token strings from full internal logits.

competitive_landscape.title: Reverse Prompt Engineering
competitive_landscape.relationship: Training-free, limited-output, black-box prompt-recovery competitor.
competitive_landscape.difference: Li and Klabjan use a genetic algorithm under strict zero-shot black-box conditions and target useful natural prompts from limited text outputs. This is operationally broader but does not claim SODA's token-exact reconstruction.

competitive_landscape.title: PTP: Previous-Token Prediction based LLM Inversion for Near-Exact Prompt Reconstruction
competitive_landscape.relationship: Post-publication black-box near-exact prompt-reconstruction successor.
competitive_landscape.difference: PTP trains a model to predict previous tokens from synthetic target outputs and frames reconstruction sequentially, moving near exactness toward black-box text access. It is later than SODA and does not require differentiating through the target model, but depends on training an auxiliary inverter.

competitive_landscape.title: An Invariant Latent Space Perspective on Language Model Inversion
competitive_landscape.relationship: Post-publication learned latent-space inversion competitor.
competitive_landscape.difference: Inv2A learns a lightweight inverse encoder with source and cycle invariance and combines multiple outputs in representation space, reporting gains over nine user/system-prompt datasets. It emphasizes semantic prompt recovery and amortization rather than SODA's exact short-token search.

competitive_landscape.title: Prompting Complexity: Shortest Prompts for Texts and Behaviors in LLMs
competitive_landscape.relationship: Post-publication formalization of observable prompt preimages.
competitive_landscape.difference: Cosma explicitly treats deterministic visible outputs as having a preimage set and asks for the shortest plausible generating prompt rather than assuming a unique historical cause. This formal lens directly exposes why SODA's text-output equality cannot certify original-prompt exactness.

competitive_landscape.title: Language Models are Injective and Hence Invertible
competitive_landscape.relationship: Post-publication exact inversion from internal hidden states with a formal guarantee.
competitive_landscape.difference: SIPIT proves almost-sure injectivity under stated decoder/parameter assumptions and sequentially recovers exact tokens from per-position hidden states in at most T times vocabulary trials. Its observation is far more internal than output logits, but it supplies the kind of uniqueness theorem and linear sequential structure SODA lacks.

competitive_landscape.title: Recovering Input Text from Hidden States: Study of Gradient-Based Inversion of Decoder-Only Language Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Post-publication continuous optimization study for exact hidden-state inversion.
competitive_landscape.difference: Slowikowski and Majewski retain continuous search until token commitment and use discrete commit loss to make failures observable, reaching 97.5% exact recovery on 10-token C4 prompts with a wider candidate window. The signal is hidden states rather than generated outputs, but its failure diagnostics and near-miss analysis are directly relevant to SODA.

competitive_landscape.title: Automatically Auditing Large Language Models via Discrete Optimization
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct discrete-optimization and target-output predecessor.
competitive_landscape.difference: ARCA jointly optimizes prompts and outputs for specified auditing behaviors and was already used to reverse fixed suffixes. SODA narrows the goal to original-input recovery and replaces coordinate approximations with relaxed one-hot Adam search.

competitive_landscape.title: Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks on Aligned Language Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Greedy Coordinate Gradient search baseline and adversarial-prompt predecessor.
competitive_landscape.difference: GCG uses token-coordinate gradients to find suffixes that induce target behaviors and can transfer across models. SODA's relaxed joint variables are much stronger for exact short-input logit inversion, although the target implements GCG under a custom matched loss and wall-time budget rather than its original jailbreak task.

competitive_landscape.title: Hard Prompts Made Easy: Gradient-Based Discrete Optimization for Prompt Tuning and Discovery
competitive_landscape.relationship: Continuous-to-discrete hard-prompt optimization predecessor.
competitive_landscape.difference: PEZ repeatedly projects continuous prompt embeddings to vocabulary tokens and optimizes controllable hard prompts. SODA instead relaxes one-hot vocabulary coordinates and matches a known LM output, adding decay and optimizer resets to improve exact recovery.

competitive_landscape.title: Gradient-based Adversarial Attacks against Text Transformers
competitive_landscape.relationship: Foundational differentiable distribution-over-tokens attack predecessor.
competitive_landscape.difference: GBDA parameterizes a distribution over text and uses gradient optimization for adversarial examples, establishing the relaxed-discrete technique family. SODA specializes it to causal-LM inversion and attributes gains to its custom Adam decay and reset dynamics.

competitive_landscape.title: Was it Slander? Towards Exact Inversion of Generative Language Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct author-team predecessor and motivating application.
competitive_landscape.difference: The earlier work uses genetic algorithms and particle-swarm optimization to ask whether a reported output has a causal prompt, concluding exact reconstruction is rare. SODA is the stronger white-box successor, but still cannot turn heuristic failure into a proof of nonexistence.

competitive_landscape.title: Uncovering Hidden Intentions: Exploring Prompt Recovery for Deeper Insights into Generated Texts
competitive_landscape.relationship: Generated-text prompt-recovery predecessor.
competitive_landscape.difference: Give et al. study recovering likely intent from generated text in an open task setting. Its semantic objective better fits explainability, while SODA's exactness target requires much stronger access and short inputs.

competitive_landscape.title: PRSA: Prompt Stealing Attacks against Real-World Prompt Services
competitive_landscape.relationship: Real-world black-box prompt-stealing attack.
competitive_landscape.difference: PRSA targets deployed prompt services and iteratively reconstructs valuable prompts through service interactions. It is operationally realistic but optimizes semantic/function similarity rather than exact historical tokens; SODA's UI discussion should not be conflated with this black-box setting.

competitive_landscape.title: Prompt Stealing Attacks Against Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Prompt-service theft predecessor using black-box interactions.
competitive_landscape.difference: Sha and Zhang infer protected prompts through queries to an LLM service, focusing on prompt assets and downstream performance. SODA focuses exact token causality under white-box gradients and full output information.

competitive_landscape.title: Prompt Inversion Attack against Collaborative Inference of Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Prompt reconstruction from split collaborative-inference leakage.
competitive_landscape.difference: Qu et al. reconstruct prompts from shared intermediate information in collaborative inference, a distinct deployment threat with stronger internal leakage than output APIs. SODA instead consumes output signals plus the complete model and provides no split-computing defense evaluation.

competitive_landscape.title: Input Reconstruction Attack against Vertical Federated Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Input reconstruction from intermediate federated representations.
competitive_landscape.difference: Zheng studies reconstructing private text from vertical-federated intermediate states. That leakage channel is not generated output and permits different inversion strategies; it demonstrates why SODA's output-access threat should remain separate from representation leakage.

competitive_landscape.title: InversionView: A General-Purpose Method for Reading Information from Neural Activations
competitive_landscape.relationship: Activation-inversion interpretability predecessor.
competitive_landscape.difference: InversionView samples inputs that produce similar activations to characterize a representation's equivalence class rather than identify one historical cause. Its set-valued interpretation is a useful conceptual corrective to SODA's unique-prompt framing.

competitive_landscape.title: InverseScope: Scalable Activation Inversion for Interpreting Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Contemporary scalable activation-inversion framework.
competitive_landscape.difference: InverseScope learns a conditional generator for distributions of activation-matching inputs and quantitatively tests feature consistency. It targets interpretable neighborhoods rather than exact output causality, and its current v3 postdates SODA with broader scaling analysis.

competitive_landscape.title: Information Leakage in Embedding Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Foundational text-reconstruction privacy attack on continuous representations.
competitive_landscape.difference: Song and Raghunathan demonstrate that text embeddings leak sensitive inputs and use relaxed token distributions for inversion. SODA transfers related optimization ideas to decoder outputs, but full logits and embeddings are distinct security boundaries.

competitive_landscape.title: IPAD: Inverse Prompt for AI Detection - A Robust and Interpretable LLM-Generated Text Detector
competitive_landscape.relationship: Post-publication application of prompt inversion to AI-text detection.
competitive_landscape.difference: IPAD predicts a plausible generating prompt and uses prompt-text alignment as interpretable detection evidence, reporting robust detector gains. It shows a useful application for approximate inverse prompts, whereas SODA's exact-token criterion and white-box access are unnecessary for that goal.

competitive_landscape.title: Trojan Detection in Large Language Models: Insights from The Trojan Detection Challenge
competitive_landscape.relationship: Backdoor-detection benchmark underlying the target's six-trigger demonstration.
competitive_landscape.difference: Maloyan et al. analyze the challenge and its detection setting across backdoored LLMs. SODA uses one released Pythia checkpoint for qualitative exact-trigger recovery but does not rerun the challenge protocol or report detector-level recall and false positives.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims the first reliable exact inversion of both natural and random language-model inputs, 79.5% random and 98.1% in-distribution recovery up to ten tokens, a new SODA optimizer that substantially beats GCG and learned inversion, scalability from 33M to 3B parameters, strong inversion from limited logits, and promising privacy, backdoor, and slander applications with zero false positives.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The strongest empirical contribution is genuine: under exact white-box access, known short length, deterministic greedy decoding, manually tuned parameters, and one full vocabulary-sized output-logit vector, SODA improves exact random-token recovery from 11.8% GCG and 3.9% learned inversion to 79.5%. Its optimizer ablation is unusually large and shows decay, resets, and omission of bias correction all matter. However, relaxed token optimization predates SODA in GBDA and PEZ, exact-output search predates it in ARCA, learned probability inversion predates it in Morris et al., and PILS appeared before the target's arXiv submission with a stronger multi-step logprob inverter. The 79.5% average masks 13.6% at length ten on TinyStories and zero at lengths nine and ten on Qwen2.5-3B; text-only inversion is 3.6%; PII exact recovery is zero; the backdoor evidence is six examples; and the appendix directly contradicts an unconditional 0% false-positive claim.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty is moderate-to-strong but narrow: SODA is plausibly the first demonstrated per-instance white-box search method to recover a large fraction of exact arbitrary short token sequences directly from generated-output logits across several decoder checkpoints. It is not a general inverse for ordinary LLM outputs, not a proof of unique causality, not a practical private-data attack as evaluated, and not a certificate for slander detection. The most reusable contribution is the optimizer design plus signal-depth/false-discovery benchmark. A stronger successor should normalize observation bits, jointly infer length, test realistic rounded top-k interfaces and model mismatch, compare against PILS/PTP/SIPIT-style sequential alternatives, extend well beyond ten tokens and 3B, publish complete result artifacts, and report posterior sets or certificates instead of treating output consistency as historical identity.

reviewer_notes: All 15 pages of the exact hash-pinned arXiv v2 PDF were read and rendered at page resolution. Every equation, algorithm, table, and figure was visually inspected: Figures 1-2; Equations 1-12; Algorithms 1-3; Tables 1-11; the convergence and position plots; the PII decomposition; all six displayed backdoor examples; and both provider-UI screenshots. The public code DOI was resolved to Zenodo concept 15539879 / record 15539880 and its sole notebook was audited byte-for-byte (SHA-256 1a25975daefa00018d38d01715cc38f81e45c9e10b79374ec54036dddb430858), including dependencies, defaults, stopping criteria, losses, seeds, result serialization, and embedded outputs. Twenty-five current primary competitors were checked through 2026-08-23 from arXiv, PMLR, and OpenReview, including post-publication PTP, Inv2A, Prompting Complexity, SIPIT, the continuous hidden-state inversion study, InverseScope, and IPAD. The current arXiv source is v2 dated 2025-11-10; the PDF title, current metadata title, and older Zenodo title differ. The duplicated reference ID was checked against official arXiv metadata: 2404.13660 is Trojan Detection, whereas Was it Slander is 2407.11059. No shared atlas projections were rebuilt.
